newsitem.title: USA: Pamela Harriman eulogized by Clinton, Democrats.
newsitem.headline: Pamela Harriman eulogized by Clinton, Democrats.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday led Americans in praising U.S. Ambassador to France Pamela Harriman after her death in Paris.

The State Department said there would be a memorial service for her in Paris and then her body -- accompanied by her son Winston Spencer Churchill -- would be transported to Washington, D.C. for a funeral, probably next week. She is to be buried at Arden House in New York State, former residence of her husband, the late Governor Averell Harriman.

Harriman had been planning to retire as ambassador in the next few months. Speculation on her successor has centred on Frank Wisner, U.S. ambassador to India, and New York investment banker Felix Rohatyn.
Harriman was "one of the most unusual and gifted people I ever met," Clinton told reporters as he left the White House for a trip to Georgia.

"She was an extaordinary U.S. ambassador ... earning the trust of the leaders (of France) and the admiration of the people," he said of the prominent Democratic party fund-raiser and Clinton supporter who died in a Paris hospital on Wednesday of a brain haemorrhage, aged 76.

"Our country will miss her," Clinton said. "We are deeply indebted to the work she did in France in maintaining our relationships with one of our oldest and closest allies. She was a source of judgment and inspiration to me, a source of constant good humour and charm and real friendship and we will miss her very very much."
Clinton termed Harriman, a British-born naturalised American citizen, "another immigrant who became a great American."
He telephoned French President Jacques Chirac from Air Force One to speak about Harriman, a spokesman told reporters.

Harriman was born in Farnborough, England, and became a U.S. citizen after marrying her third husband, the late multimillionaire diplomat Averell Harriman, in 1971. She was a daughter-in-law of the late British Prime Minister Winston Churchill by her first marriage.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told a news briefing that "America has lost a remarkable representative, the State Department has lost one of its most effective diplomats and I have lost a friend."
"She was a central figure in the history of this century," Albright said.

"In the capital of America's oldest ally she played an important role in our shared effort to bring peace to Bosnia and to pursue President Clinton's highest priority -- to forge a Europe that would be, for the first time, fully united, fully secure and fully free.
"Amid the high tech gadgetry of the information age, she was a master of the personal touch that separates simple communications from true diplomacy," Albright said.

Senate minority leader Tom Daschle told reporters that "Pamela Harriman was a giant. She was a woman of extraordinary talent and ability and respect worldwide, not just in this country. Obviously, as a Democrat she was a woman who was extraordinarily proud of the partisan roots and philisophic approach that our party represents."
"But she was less known as a partisan than, in my view, a statesman at the end. There is no doubt we have lost a true American patriot."
Former ambassador to the Soviet Union and Democratic Party chairman Bob Strauss called her "a hard working, substantive ambassador."
"Averell and Pam helped get me elected head of the Democratic Party," he recalled. "She was an elegant lady."

Sen. Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat, said "Pamela Harriman's life was one usually reserved for the storybooks. Pamela Harriman was proud of her British roots but even prouder to be an American. She loved this country and stood up for America with dignity."
